opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, I didn't really have to "sell" it in the traditional sense, and I think that's the key point. The strongest case wasn't a pitch deck. It was the work we'd already done together.

By the time we were talking seriously about starting a company, we had spent a long time building an open-source project side by side. We'd been through late nights fixing bugs before releases and arguing about design decisions on GitHub. We had dealt with users from all over the world filing issues at three in the morning. So when you go to someone and say, "Let's do this as a company," you're not asking them to trust a stranger's vision. You're asking them to continue something they've already seen work, with people whose strengths and weaknesses they already know.

The argument I made was roughly three parts.

First, the timing. Inference was becoming the real bottleneck. Everyone was excited about training bigger models, but once those models exist, someone has to serve them cheaply, quickly and reliably at enormous scale. That problem was only going to get bigger, and we were one of the few teams already sitting right at the center of it.

Second, sustainability. An open-source project at this scale can't run forever on goodwill, student time and a few sponsors. If we wanted the project to keep improving, and to stay open, we needed a structure that could hire full-time engineers and invest for the long term. A company was a way to protect what we'd built, not abandon it. I think that mattered a lot to everyone. Nobody wanted to feel like they were "cashing out" the community.

Third, honestly, the team itself. I said something like: "Look, we've already proven we can build something people actually use. The hardest part of a startup is finding people you can work with under pressure, and we've already passed that test." That's rare. Many founders meet, get along over coffee, and then discover a year later that they can't make decisions together. We'd already had our fights and survived them.

Of course there were real concerns: whether we were giving up academic careers, whether commercial pressure would conflict with the open-source community, and whether we were technical people who knew nothing about running a business. I didn't pretend those weren't risks. I think being honest about them made the conversation more credible. In the end it felt less like convincing someone and more like all of us realizing we were already halfway down that road.

r001.rationale: The response discusses the project’s sustainability, team, and risks, but does not ask whether the prospective co-founder would be happy becoming wealthy without joining if the LLM project failed.

fable-5.1.text:
I'll answer as the guest directly.

Honestly, I didn't really have to make much of a case, because the case made itself. When I was talking to him, I said, look, vLLM is already one of the most widely used inference engines in the world. Every day there are so many people pulling the code, deploying it, running their models on it. The usage is there, the community is there, the engineering reputation is there. What's missing is a team that can take that, do it full-time, and turn it into something enterprises can actually rely on.

And the second thing I said was about timing. Inference is going to be the bottleneck of this whole wave. Training is something a few big labs do, but inference is something everybody does, every single time a model is called. The cost of inference is where the real money and the real pain is. So if you believe models are going to be used more and more, you have to believe inference infrastructure is a huge opportunity.

Then the third point was the team. We're not people who learned about this from the outside. We're the ones who wrote a lot of the core code, who've been answering issues from users at two in the morning, who know exactly where the system breaks and why. That kind of hands-on understanding is very hard to buy or hire. So I told him, if you're going to bet on someone doing this, it makes sense to bet on the people who already built it.

And I think what convinced him in the end wasn't any single argument. It was that he looked at the community, saw how much people trusted it, and realized that trust is the hardest part to create from zero. We already had it.

r001.rationale: The response does not ask whether the prospective co-founder would be happy becoming wealthy without joining if the LLM project failed. It instead describes the project's usage, opportunity, team, and community trust.

astra-6.text:
I think the case comes down to three things: why this problem matters, why this team can solve it, and why it’s worth doing now. You need to make those concrete enough that the other person can form their own judgment.

And it has to be a two-way conversation. What do they want to build? What risks are they comfortable taking? Where do they disagree with you? You’re not just trying to convince someone to join—you’re trying to find out whether you can build a company together.

r001.rationale: The response discusses the problem, team, timing, and two-way fit, but does not ask whether the prospective co-founder would be happy becoming wealthy without joining if the LLM project failed.

I’d explain what we wanted to build, why I thought it mattered, and what our team could bring. But I also wanted to understand what they were looking for. Why start a company? What would make this worth committing to? Ideally, it becomes a conversation about what we could build together.
